title: Milarepa's remorse
hook: Milarepa used black magic to take revenge, then turned to the teaching in remorse

segments.voice: Yesterday, Marpa the farmer-translator, walking to India and back for the teaching. Your line was three journeys. What did you go the distance for? Day nine hundred seventy-two.

A saint Tibetans hold dear begins his story as a killer. That's not a rumor; it's how his life story tells it. Milarepa was a boy when his father died. His uncle and aunt took charge of the family's fields and house, promising to hand them back when the boy grew up. They didn't. The widow and her children were left to work as servants on their own land, in rags. His mother never forgot it. And when Milarepa was grown, she put a demand to him that would change everything. Today: Milarepa's remorse.
screen: `A FATHER DIES.` → `AN UNCLE TAKES THE FIELDS.` → `A MOTHER'S DEMAND.`

segments.voice: First, the revenge. His mother sent him to learn black magic, and told him, in the story, that if he failed she would take her own life. He learned it. At the uncle's house, during a wedding feast, the building collapsed and many guests died, though the uncle and aunt survived. His mother rejoiced. When the villagers turned against her, he called down a hailstorm on their fields. Second, the turn. Milarepa didn't. The biography says he was filled with remorse: he couldn't sleep, couldn't eat, couldn't stop seeing what he had done. In Buddhist teaching, actions bring their results, and he knew that what he had set in motion would follow him. Third, what remorse does here. It doesn't stop at guilt. Guilt can just sit on a person. Milarepa's remorse got up and went looking. He sought out a teacher, then another, and finally heard the name Marpa, and the story says the name alone moved him to tears. Fourth, why the story starts there. Tibetans could have told the life of a saint who was always good. Instead they keep the worst part in, at the start, in full. As teachers tell it, the message is plain: no one is too far gone to turn back. The harm is real; the story never pretends otherwise. But the turn is real too. Milarepa will spend years paying for what he did, as we'll see tomorrow. The question it leaves is a small one. Not what's the worst thing you've done, but where is one harm you could stop today, and turn from?
screen: `BLACK MAGIC, AT HIS MOTHER'S DEMAND.` · `REMORSE: NO SLEEP, NO FOOD.` · `REMORSE THAT GOES LOOKING.` · `THE WORST PART, KEPT IN.` · then, large: `HE TURNED BACK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: turn from one harm. Settle, and breathe. Without digging for anything heavy, notice one small way you've been causing harm lately: a sharp tone, a habit, a word about someone behind their back. Name it plainly to yourself. If there's a sting, let it be there, without flinching. Then picture yourself turning, the way a person turns on a road. One harm, set down. Rest in the breath. The bell holds the time.
Milarepa's remorse. The sorrow over his revenge that didn't stop at guilt, but sent him looking for a teacher. Today's word.
Your line: he turned back. Today, stop one small harm for a full day, and notice what it's like without it. Day nine hundred seventy-two.

howItsDone: Milarepa's life story is read and retold in Tibetan Buddhist communities, and teachers use its opening, revenge and remorse, to show that even serious wrongdoing can be turned from through regret, purification and practice.

myth: Milarepa's biography leaves out his crimes to protect his name
it keeps them in, at the start, in full.
his remorse led him to search for a teacher
it didn't stop at guilt; it sent him looking, finally to Marpa.
Milarepa's mother regretted the revenge too
in the story she rejoiced. the remorse was his.

fork.setup: you're Milarepa. your revenge has worked: the house has fallen and the fields are ruined. your mother is celebrating. what do you do?
options: celebrate with her; justice is done.
try to forget it and move on.
let the remorse send you to find a teacher.
fork.reveal: Milarepa couldn't sleep or eat for remorse, and went looking for a teacher, finally finding Marpa.

original.note: Sanskrit for regret; in some Abhidharma lists it can be wholesome or not, depending on what it regrets.

trapdoor: what you thought: a saint who felt bad once.
what it means: a man who killed in revenge, and whose remorse sent him looking for a way to turn back.
what a scholar hears: a biography that keeps the worst part in, so the turn from harm becomes the heart of the story.
recall: the practice of yoga, the meditators' path

sources.ref: The Life of Milarepa (Tsangnyön Heruka), the early chapters

notes: Hook avoids a superlative ('a saint Tibetans hold dear').

Story beats (father's death, uncle and aunt seize the estate, mother's threat, collapse at the wedding feast with the uncle and aunt surviving, hailstorm, remorse, hearing Marpa's name) paraphrased from the Life of Milarepa. The number killed is deliberately not stated.
'Killer' in the hook is blunt; confirm a Keeper is comfortable with it.
Sanskrit kaukṛtya (Pali kukkucca): in Asanga's Abhidharmasamuccaya it is one of the variable factors. Confirm spelling, stress and the gloss.
Audit: order corrected to the Life: the mother rejoices after the collapse, and the hailstorm follows when the villagers threaten her.

Editor: 'father's brother and his wife' changed to 'uncle and aunt' (the Life names a paternal uncle and aunt; the aunt is not the uncle's wife in standard accounts); framed the lesson as the teachers' message rather than the narrator's; varied the 'ordinary day' turn; practice no longer tells the listener what they feel.
